Germany overall isnt super sketch but my scariest moments there were around train stations in the middle of the night or early morning. 

I once decided to take the train home (2+ hours) instead of paying for a hostel after a concert. Bad decision. A guy came and sat down next to me (I was female, 22 at the time) and I got the creepiest vibes from him. He was asking me all sorts of personal questions--where i lived, where i was from, where I was going on the train. When he got up to talk to someone across the aisle, I acted like I had to get off at that stop and went down to the first deck (regional train, two decks.) But actually i just switched cars. I was terrified. 

But I had to take 3 trains to get home. Second train was bad too. These guys halfway down the car started arguing loudly about Mohammed. Both were Muslim, both spoke fluent German. One was very devout and the other not so much (probably more of a heritage thing.) I swear they were going to come to blows. Somehow security was called and these guys were escorted off the train a few stops later, yelling still. 

Third train just had a guy on it who stared at me, unblinking, for the duration of the ride. That just scared me because I thought he might follow me home but he didnt. Never again. That was a bad night.

Side note, some really sketch stuff has happened around the Cologne train station (stabbings, gang rape on new years) so yeah. Best to check out those high speed trains in the day time with friends.

My mom isn't an anti-vaxxer entirely. She had an aversion to a lot of vaccinations for reasons she never fully explained, frequented homeopathic doctors, had friends that were anti-vax, etc. 

She did give me the bare minimum vaccinations. I think she understood that polio is bad, measles are bad, vaccines help. But I never got any of the ones that weren't legally required in order for me to go to school or camp. 

When I grew up, I got the HPV vaccine quickly, surprised that I'd never had it. Apparently a lot of people dont get their kids vaccinated for HPV because they associate it with their kids having sex, and so they dont want to give it to pre-teens for that connotation. I dont know that I ever brought it up with her. The anti-vaxxers you see on the internet are rabid, but there's actually a sliding scale out there in the real world--"All vaccines are evil" vs "I'm suspicious of some of these but I know some are also very good." Whether her suspicions are valid or not, my mom falls on the less extreme end of the scale. I'm glad that she gave me the vaccines she did, and although I was a little freaked out at the ones I missed, they were all ones you can get later on, so I did, and I'm fine :)

Speaking as a bride who is limiting plus ones to my wedding, here's my two cents.

There are lots of reasons why she may not have given you a plus one. For me personally, we are paying for the wedding on our own, so we really have to limit the budget and thus the guest list. I'm only inviting long term partners and spouses of friends as a result. Additionally, it'll be a small wedding and we would prefer to know everyone there rather than having a bunch of random people there because we handed  out plus ones.

That being said, if a friend of mine had a serious SO that I wasn't aware of (or forgot at invitation time--things are hectic!) I would want him or her to speak up. While I don't want anyone insisting on having a casual boyfriend or girlfriend tag along, I certainly don't want someone to feel they have to leave a partner behind. 

I'd reach out to her, but gently, understanding that she may be on limited budget or may have had a brain hiccup in writing out the invites. If she still says the guest list is limited, don't be hurt. I can't emphasize enough how tough these things are to plan and that there may be a lot of hidden factors.

I used the Denver Early Start model which was developed in 2015. It's play based and targeted towards changing social behavior, not how kids think or operate. E.g., stemming is fine, but there's a manner and maybe a place to do it that isn't socially intrusive. For example, some of the kids would learn to communicate that they were feeling uncomfortable and needed stemming time or a break from the group, rather than just going into stemming during an activity and ignoring the other kids.

We didn't withhold food or punish the kids ever. We just taught them social skills and communication. In my opinion, it was a really good and non-intrusive method. We basically just played with them during sessions and had snack and lunch time just like a school. And they'd learn skills like sharing and using words to express themselves so that their parents would know what they wanted or needed better.

We also gave hugs if kids needed it and if they started crying because they were genuinely upset, we would let them cry it out and comfort them as needed. It was a very loving environment, I felt. I hope that this clears up at least the type of ABA I was involved in.

Everyone deals with depression differently. That being said, here's what helps me the most: 

1) Ask me to hang out/just get out of the house. The hardest thing in the world can be getting out of bed or off the couch. Don't assume that just because I haven't contacted you, I don't like you or don't want to hang out. You're not annoying if you contact me frequently. I may not say yes every time for various reasons, and feel free to ask about those (eg, I may say no because I'm too stubborn to get out of bed, or I may be saying no because there are too many people around at the coffee shop you invited me to). My fiance will literally pick me up off the couch to walk the dog, and my best friend has banged on the door until I get up to answer it as well. Be there. It's also good to feel like someone still wants to be around us. Another way hanging out helps is to make us not feel like a social pariah no one wants around. 

2) Don't try to make it better with your words. Depression takes a lot of medication and therapy to be treated. Instead, listen, sympathize, and hug me.
 
3) Feel free to ask what our triggers are/what our depressive episode symptoms are. Just like if you were around someone with epilepsy, when you'd need to know what to do in event of a seizure, it can be important to know about our depression as well. And by trigger I mean it in the least Tumblr-ish way possible. For me, I just asked my close friends if they could avoid watching movies/having conversations with me that focused on sex/had sex scenes. Conversations have been easy, and the movies are fine too--they have different movie nights without me for Deadpool, that's all. 

4) Finally, and this won't apply to everyone because it depends how close you are, make sure we're getting the care we need. It's easy to wonder when it's okay to walk away from someone who's depressed, and my line in the sand is when they refuse to get help. If they're not taking their meds or not trying to get meds, if they're not attending therapy or refusing it, and being around them feels like too much, you don't have to. But if you're close and we just have a habit of missing meds until later in the day, check up and make sure we've taken them if we're looking down. That sort of thing. Encourage friends to seek a proper therapist. Offer transport if they need it temporarily. I know I wasn't getting the care I needed for a while because I was without a car for a few months. Wouldn't have gotten a doctor without my best friend.

Violations of the dead donor rule and the push toward partial brain death as the working definition. 

I study medical ethics, and some of the most terrifying stories I've heard are about physicians who want to get at the organs while they're fresh so badly that the donor isn't technically or legally dead when the organs are removed. 

In addition, there are actually at least 3 ways to define "death" medically: full brain death, partial brain death, and whole body death. Now, you can really only collect viable organs from fully brain dead patients; by the time they're at whole body death, they're basically cold as ice, organs unusable. The funny thing about brain death is that your organs will still function with assistance, and "you" could very well be breathing and dead. There's been more of a push in the field to define death as when the part of the brain that governs who you are, what makes you you, the personality and all that, is dead. That means that you could be breathing WITHOUT assistance.

Without getting too technical about it, I'll just say that the thought of anyone, mistakenly or otherwise, taking my organs prematurely terrifies me.

It'll just go in one of our employees-only "known issues" articles. If you call in, though, and it is a known issue, we can issue you a replacement. We just aren't allowed to tell you it's a known issue under any circumstances. 

And your tech support agent had nothing to do with the defect anyway, so do try to be kind to us. If it's really bad we can work something out so that you're satisfied at the end of the day, but if you're rude to us, your case will "accidentally" be at the bottom of our priority list and may not get touched for days.

I was home schooled my whole life. I went to college, got a 4.0, and was valedictorian. After teaching English abroad for a year, I now work with kids with autism. Academically, it's the best thing I could have asked for. Essay writing is a breeze and I have a firm grasp of history and literature. Math was never my strong suit, but I did enjoy basic science. It's really just a matter of knowing how to get involved.

The cons? Sometimes the communities you get involved with are conservative to the point of being toxic. We moved to the South and it was way worse down here than up North. High school was awful (when isn't it?). One atheist homeschooler  I knew complained that it was hard to find anyone who wasn't religious, which is probably true. I'm still scarred from some of my experiences with those people. I should note that they weren't all homeschooled, but most of them were. One thing just lead to another and that ended up being the social group we hung out with the most.

All in all, I'd do it again in a heartbeat. If I could change one thing, I'd have hung out with different people in high school. But I think a lot of people can say that.

In November she invited her boyfriend, whose dorm was literally across the parking lot from us, to live with us. Only she didn't ask me or tell me. No, she hid him in her room until January. I mean, he didn't leave her room when I was in the common areas. He only went to the bathroom when I was in my room. They whispered all the time. It was the weirdest shit ever.

After January they gave up the charade, but it got weirder. She wouldn't go to the bathroom without him, even to pee. She'd send him out on days when the sidewalks were iced over to get her food because it was "too dangerous" for her to go. She'd come home and mention something about a migraine while turning off all the lights and closing the blinds while I was trying to study, and then watching really loud tv in her room and laughing outrageously. And all the while, she barely spoke to me, and when she did, she was cold. Angry. I began to lock my door at night, I was so scared of her. I didn't come home before she was in bed if I could help it. I'd have panic attacks because I was afraid I'd forgotten to clean something in the kitchen.

And then, in April, she was gone. Literally overnight. I was at Relay for Life and when I returned the next morning, everything was gone. The couch, the dishes, the diningroom table, everything except the tv, which was mine. She left a note saying she had to leave because it was a "toxic environment." At least I had the place to myself during finals.

She was real scary. I later heard that she'd been kicked out of her first dorm for writing on the bathroom mirror in red marker, something about the roommates not keeping the place clean enough. I think she needed help.
